body:
PR #913 (`Refs #900`) makes `cargo xtask gate` use sccache as a shared compile cache when it is on PATH, and lightens the dev profile (line-table debug info for our crates, none for dependencies, dependency `opt-level` 1). It was written and measured on Windows only; the maintainers have no macOS machine. This issue is for a contributor on macOS.

What to do, on the PR's branch (`issue/900-build-cache`) or on `main` once #913 is merged:
1. Without sccache installed: `cargo xtask gate quick --dry-run` and one real `cargo xtask gate test <any test name>` - the gate must run exactly as before (no wrapper set, no error).
2. Install sccache, then build the same test binary from an empty `target/` twice in two different checkouts or worktrees: note the cold time, the second (warm cache) time, the `sccache --show-stats` hit rate and the `target/` size. Do not export `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` as an environment variable (sccache hashes `CARGO_*` variables; on Windows that gave 0 cross-worktree hits).
3. Check the opt-outs: `CAMCRAFT_NO_SCCACHE=1` and a pre-set `RUSTC_WRAPPER` must both win.
4. Check a panic backtrace of a failing test still shows file:line with the new debug settings.
5. Is the C code (flecs, built through `cc`) cached on macOS? On Windows/MSVC it is not.

Report the numbers and anything that broke as a comment here (and on #913 if it is still open). A fix, if one is needed, is a small PR against `xtask/` (a process file: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`).

Windows numbers for comparison are in PR #913's body.

Done means: the five points above are answered for macOS in a comment, and any breakage has a PR or its own issue.

title: Reduced-fidelity models: tighten the laws that only refuse today (turning, rotary, multi-axis, cone and engrave rides), the collision laws, and give the import budget a setting

labels.name: enhancement

labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: area:multiaxis
labels.description: 3+2, 5-axis, rotary

labels.name: area:turning
labels.description: Lathe and mill-turn

labels.name: area:sim
labels.description: Stock simulation and verification

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
Found while working #864 (a STEP model imported coarser than the importer promises is flagged, its gouge verdicts tightened, and refused past that).

**What #864's PR does.** A reduced-fidelity model carries its achieved error. The gouge laws of the upright mill kinds subtract the excess from their tolerance while a positive tolerance is left: the section law (b), the solid law (b2), the envelope law's gouge half (f), `generate::contain_into`, the lathe's axial hole verdict, and the program sim's deviation tolerance. Past that, the program gate refuses by name.

**What is owed.** Everything below is safe today (refused, or stricter than before), but less useful than it should be.

1. **Kinds refused outright on any reduced-fidelity model**, because their gouge laws do not read the excess yet (`operation::fidelity_law::excess_aware`):
   - the cone and engrave rides: 2D chamfer, deburr, trace, engrave (generator construction laws);
   - probe, and the cross drill (`operation/cross_part.rs`, `SolidLaw { allow: GOUGE_TOL }`);
   - the multi-axis kinds (`motion` `multiaxis/entry_ramp.rs`, `stamp*.rs`, `rotary_links.rs`) and the rotary kinds (`operation/rotary_law.rs`, `allow` and `rapid_allow`);
   - turning (`motion` `turning/revolve.rs`, `form.rs`, `thread.rs`; `blade_warnings`, `thread_warnings`, `form_warnings`);
   - plasma.
   Each needs `material.excess` threaded into its law and the kind added to `excess_aware`. A metre-unit STEP file is always reduced fidelity (next point), so these kinds cannot post on one today.
2. **Collision laws are not tightened**: shank and holder reach (`sim` `verify/reach.rs`), rapids in stock (`verify/rapids.rs`, `rapids_posed.rs`, `rapids_radial.rs`), the turning rapid, bar-feed and holder scans (`margin: GOUGE_TOL` in `generate.rs`). They judge clearance against rest material. While an operation still posts the excess is under 0.01 mm, so a clearance can read up to that much too generous on a convex wall.
3. **A metre-unit STEP file** stops at the kernel's least tolerance (1e-5 m = 0.01 mm, #839) and is flagged reduced fidelity with half the verdict tolerance left. Scaling the geometry to millimetres before meshing would remove the cause.
4. **The facet budget is not a user setting.** The refusal says "re-import with a larger budget" (the maintainer's wording on #864), but `MAX_FACETS` is a constant. The import dialog, the script verb and MCP `import_model` need a budget the user can raise.
5. **Display tolerances** still read the plain 0.01 mm on a reduced-fidelity model: the machined-surface classes (`machined_classes.rs`) and the viewport preview (`ui` `trace/eye.rs`, `cpu_eye.rs`). The binding verdict is tightened; the colours are not.
6. **The envelope law (f) and the containment solid law** are tightened through the same helper as (b) but have no fixture-level pin of their own on a reduced-fidelity model.

Done means: each kind in (1) is either judged with tightened laws or stays refused for a stated reason; the laws in (2) grow their bands by the excess; (3) and (4) are decided and built or closed with the reason; pins for (6).

body:
Maintainer decision (2026-11-11, in chat, on #901): "the units should come from a 'global setup' rather than a localized setup with operations or the machine settings.. all machines can handle mm and inch and degrees and radians.. just a matter of post output.. that setting should come from a global setting for the document rather than machine or post."

Today: the posted unit comes from the machine file (`kinematics.default.units.length` -> `machine.units`), and only the three Tormach posts read it. The document's Units choice (`SetUnits`, a radio on the Stock page) is display-only. So the user cannot find where the program's unit is set, and most posts cannot post inch at all.

Wanted:
- One document-level setting decides the unit of the posted program for every post. Recommended: the document's existing Units choice (`SetUnits`, already saved in the project file and already an undoable command with history) becomes the program unit too - one setting, not two. A second, separate derivation anywhere (machine file, post option, setup, operation) is a bug.
- The machine file's `units.length` only says which unit the file's own numbers are written in (the parser already scales them to mm); it no longer chooses the program unit. The Tormach posts switch from `machine.units` to the document's unit.
- Every post writes the program in the document's unit: inch = lengths / 25.4 at four decimals, feeds and other length-bearing words converted, and the dialect's unit word (G20 / G21, Heidenhain G70 / G71, Sinumerik G70 / G71 or G700 / G710) in the opening block. A post whose control cannot run a unit (Carvera's firmware halts on G20) refuses that document by name instead.
- The setting lives where a user looks for a document-wide choice (not only on the Stock page), and the post dialog states the unit the program will be written in.
- MCP: the existing units tool (or a new one, `area:mcp`) covers it; `EndUnits` (#596) keeps working against the document's unit.

Open point for the maintainer: angles. Every post writes rotary words in degrees today and nothing in the document chooses an angle unit. If a document-level angle unit (degrees / radians) is wanted for display or output, say so and it is filed as its own issue; it is not part of this one.

Depends on #901 (each post states the unit it writes) - land that first.

Done means: with the document set to inch, each shipped post either writes a correct inch program with its unit word (golden per post, numbers checked against the mm golden / 25.4) or refuses by name; with it set to mm, output is unchanged apart from #901's unit word; no post reads `machine.units` for the program unit; the setting is reachable at document level in the UI and through MCP.

title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

title: Tool library import can't update or replace existing tools (it renames duplicates)

labels.name: enhancement

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

body:
Tool library import can't update or replace tools; it only adds or renames them.

**Where:** `ImportTools` (`crates/app/src/commands/tool_import.rs:81-86`) skips an identical tool and RENAMES a same-named different one (`A (2)`). There's no replace or update mode, and no key but the name.

**Effect:** re-importing an updated library (e.g. after a feeds-and-speeds revision) adds a renamed duplicate of every changed tool, instead of updating them. *Guess:* that's every tool in a library-wide feeds change.

**Fix sketch:** an import mode with three options: add (today's behaviour), update matching tools, or replace. Matching is by name, or by part number once tools carry one (see the tool-metadata issue filed alongside this). It's one undoable command, with a preview of what changes. Add it to MCP too.

Effort: medium.

**Done means:** re-importing a revised library updates matching tools in place, with one undo; pinned.

A tool can't store a part number, vendor, coating, helix or free-text notes.

**Where:** `ToolDto` (`crates/app/src/project/file.rs:292`) has no free-text or vendor fields.

**Effect:** tool libraries built from catalogs have to cram the part number, coating and other facts into the tool's name, e.g. `<vendor> <part#> 1/4" 4FL flat AlTiN LOC 3/4 OAL 2-1/2`. They can't be searched, sorted or shown in a setup sheet's tool list. Reordering a tool means reading the name.

**Fix:** optional fields `part_number`, `vendor`, `coating`, `helix_deg` and `notes` on the tool, as an additive key so old files load unchanged. Show them in the tool editor and on the setup sheet's tool list, and add them to MCP.

Effort: medium (data only, no geometry).

**Done means:** the fields round-trip through `.camproj` and `.camtools`, show on the setup sheet, and are editable via UI and MCP; pinned.

body:
Hole-making tools beyond the twist drill have no kind, and drills get no feeds-and-speeds suggestion.

**Where:**
- `ToolKind` has `Drill` only: no reamer, spot drill, countersink or combined center drill.
- `tabulated()` (`crates/app/src/cutting.rs:41`) excludes `Drill`, so CamCraft suggests no feeds for any drill.

**Effect:**
- A reamer can't be stored with its semantics: no chamfer lead, finish allowance, or slower speed.
- Spot drills are stored as drills, so their geometry is right but there's no "spot to a chamfer diameter" behaviour.
- No drill gets a starting rpm/feed from the cutting table.

**Fix sketch:**
- Reamer, spot drill, countersink and center drill kinds, with their op behaviours: ream at a reduced speed with a set allowance; spot or countersink to a stated diameter.
- Drill rows in the cutting table: feed per rev by diameter and material, as conservative handbook-range values.

Effort: high.

**Done means:** a reamer and a spot drill can be stored and used with their behaviour; drills get a suggested rpm/feed; pinned.

Effort: max.

The chamfer/taper kind is a sharp cone only: no tip diameter, no tip radius, and no tapered flank above a non-sharp tip.

**Fix sketch:** `Taper` gains an optional tip diameter and tip radius (and a tip form: flat or ball). The chamfer-depth math, the sim and the gouge laws use the real tip.

Effort: max (geometry).

**Done means:** a flat-tip chamfer and a radiused-point V-bit chamfer to the right width at the right depth; pinned.

body:
The turning insert model is the nose circle only: insert shape, approach (lead) angle, clearance and a sharp nose aren't modelled.

**Where:** the `Turning` kind reads only `nose_radius`, and `is_sane` requires `nose_radius > 0` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs:268`).

**Effect:**
- A 35° V insert and an 80° C insert of the same nose radius are the same tool to CamCraft. So are a 93° and a 72.5° neutral holder.
- A sharp-nose insert (0 radius, used for fine finishing and small diameters) is refused outright.
- Flank clearance isn't judged. *Guess:* back-turning or profiling a shoulder with a narrow-angle insert could rub the trailing flank unseen.

**Fix sketch:** model the insert from its ISO 1832 designation (a public standard): shape and included angle, clearance, IC and nose radius; plus the holder's approach angle and hand. Judge the full insert outline in the turning envelope and gouge laws. Allow a sharp nose with an explicit minimum.

Effort: max (geometry plus the collision laws).

**Done means:** an insert's outline (not just its nose circle) is swept by the turning verdicts; a profile the insert's flank can't reach is refused by name; pinned.

- Operations derive S/F, or G96/G95 on posts that state CSS.
- Old files load unchanged.

Effort: high, since it changes posted S/F words.

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
A tool library file (`.camtools`) can't carry a tool's drawn holder body.

**Where:** `parse_tool_library` (`crates/app/src/tool_library.rs:109`) goes through `project::tool_from_json` and `ToolDto::to_tool` (`crates/app/src/project/file.rs:462`). It returns a `Tool`, which has no body field (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs:137`), and export writes `body: None` (`file.rs:456`). A library tool can only carry the `holder_d`/`holder_len` cylinder.

**Effect:** a library meant for one machine's holders (e.g. BT30 ER20, TTS ER20 from the built-in holder library) has to carry an envelope cylinder sized to the holder's largest diameter and length instead (e.g. Ø46 × 60 for BT30). That over-reports: an ER20 nut of Ø35 under a Ø46 flange reads as Ø46 all the way down. It's safe, but it gives false hits near walls, and the user must re-pick every tool's holder by hand.

**Fix:** let `.camtools` entries carry the tool body (the drawn holder profile and the built-in holder's name), round-tripped exactly like a `.camproj` tool. An older file without it still loads.

**Done means:** export then import of a tool with a built-in holder keeps its profile bit-identical; pinned.

body:
Found during the review of PR #860 (#33, C unwind), where the lathe post got this cap.

**What happens:** `assets/posts/fanuc.cps` (about lines 109-114) and `assets/posts/doosan-dnm.cps` (about line 287) write a C word on a combined linear + rotary move at the operation's F, with no check against the rotary rate the machine file states. A short linear move with a large C change can therefore command the rotary far faster than its stated maximum.

**What #860 does for the lathe post:** `assets/posts/fanuc-lathe.cps` (`liveMove`) caps F on every C block so that the linear part does not exceed the machine's stated linear feed and the C part does not exceed its stated C rate (deg/min; the rotary `speeds` are passed to the script by `crates/post/src/post/machine.rs`), with zero-length guards. Where the machine file states no C rate, C is uncapped by data.

**Expected:** every post that writes a rotary word on a combined move applies the same rule from the same machine data (one helper, not a copy per post), or refuses by name where it cannot. Check the other dialects that can emit A/B/C on a combined move as well (tormach.cps for the microARC A, the 5-axis posts).

**Open question for the fix:** how each control reads F on a combined move (linear feed with the rotary carried along, a combined rate, or inverse time G93) - the cap must match the feed mode the post declares; cite the control's public documentation per dialect.

Done means: no posted block can command a rotary above its stated rate or a linear axis above the stated feed; pinned per dialect by a test that reads every posted block back; existing goldens move only where a block was over the limit, each listed.

Safety floor (posted G-code): effort high, high-tier review.

body:
Found during the review of PR #863 (#692).

**What happens:** the MCP feature listing reports a face's `facing` from its normal (`crates/app/src/mcp/features.rs`, `facing()`). On the cylinder-boss fixture used by `crates/app/tests/mcp_pick.rs`, BOTH flat caps of the cylinder come back as "up". The new test in PR #863 had to pick the bottom cap by its Z height instead (helper `flat_face`).

**Expected:** the top cap reads "up", the bottom cap "down".

**Why it matters:** an agent driving CamCraft through MCP chooses faces by `facing` for side-dependent work - `locate_part` mates, `lay_part_on_points`, work-offset picks, op geometry. A bottom face reported as "up" can put a part on the wrong side with no refusal.

**To find out first:** whether the fixture's STL has its bottom cap wound upward (then the fixture is wrong and a test with a correctly wound model must show "down"), or `facing()` does not take the normal from the facet winding / takes its absolute value (then the tool is wrong). Check with a model whose winding is known to be right (a box from the test helpers, and an imported STEP).

Done means: for a closed solid with correct winding, a downward-facing flat face reads "down" in every MCP tool that reports `facing`, pinned by a test with a cylinder and a box; if the fixture's winding was the cause, the fixture is fixed and the height-only `flat_face` helper in `mcp_pick.rs` can go back to using `facing`.

title: Adaptive growth planner: the ring opening is quadratic in outline vertices - one level of the user's STEP bore grows for ~200 s

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: blocked
labels.description: Waiting on another issue or a decision

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Found while reworking #850 (PR #865).

**What happens:** app `pocket3d_hsm::the_users_bore_roughs_adaptive_level_by_level_and_verifies_clean` (heavy lane, `testdata/models/Milling-test.step`). On main, one level's growth plan spends **~200 s in release** in `adaptive/grow.rs`: 33 revolutions, 157 trial steps, about 1.3 s per trial.

**Where the time goes** (local probe, release):
- 99 % of it is `rings::open`, the morphological opening: two `offset_fine` calls at `ARC_TOL` 2.5e-4 mm per trial, plus one per revolution for `whole`.
- The stock walk takes 0.6 s.
- The cleared-area offset and the intersect take 0.2 s each.

The opening's cost grows about with the **square** of the ring's vertex count. Measured cost per (vertices per trial)^2:

| fixture | vertices per trial | ns per (vertices)^2 |
|---|---|---|
| 60 x 14 slot | ~290 | ~63 |
| 60 x 40 island | ~700 | ~105 |
| the bore (fine STEP tessellation) | ~4,700 | ~58 |

So a finely tessellated outline turns a 33-revolution plan into minutes.

**Why it is not bounded:** #850's budget cannot refuse it without changing a plan that finishes on main. Measured on any time-faithful unit, the bore is the most expensive plan of all, so it stays law 2's (length) alone. See `docs/decisions/850-adaptive-geometry-budget.md`.

**Options:**
- Simplify the cleared area and the ring to the planner's working tolerance before the opening. Douglas-Peucker at the `MERGE` / `ARC_TOL` scale would remove the boolean engine's arc-tolerance vertices that say nothing about the shape.
- An opening that does not re-tessellate every convex vertex at `ARC_TOL`.
- An incremental opening.

Each option changes toolpaths: under the safety floor, with every adaptive fixture re-measured.

**Done means:** the bore's growth level plans in seconds (stated bound, release and debug) with the load, crossing and kink laws held. Every adaptive fixture's change is measured and named in the PR.

Related: #850, #44, #845.

title: Carry machined stock into a setup turned side-on (90° about X or Y)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:sim
labels.description: Stock simulation and verification

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max
labels.description: New algorithms, formats or open design (issue-worker-max)

labels.name: P8
labels.description: Larger idea needing design or research before code

body:
Part of #866. Related: #637 (carried stock on the field engine), #586.

**What the reporter wanted:** a plate modelled lying flat; Setup1 machines it flat, Setup2 stands it on its edge (part alignment "turned X -90°") and takes "What Setup1 leaves behind" as its stock. Today that carry is refused by design (`CARRY_TURN_REFUSAL`): the carried body is a two-sided column lattice (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/carry.rs`, `LatticeTurn`), which can only be re-indexed through flips over X or Y and quarter turns about Z. A side-on turn would need a re-sample at the grid pitch, and the sim refuses rather than guess.

Investigation for #866 confirmed the frame composition is right: `setup_relative::transform_between` uses the RELATIVE turn (`A_to * A_from^-1`), so two setups holding the part alike (both turned X -90°) carry fine (pinned by `setup_stock_source::both_setups_turned_alike_carry_through_the_identity`). Only a real side-on turn between the setups is refused.

**The work:** carry the machined stock through any rigid turn between setups (at least the side-on quarter turns about X and Y - the common "machine the edge" re-clamp), once the carried body lives on the field engine (#637), with the verdicts proven exact enough and the named refusal kept for anything the engine still cannot carry.

**Done means:** Setup1 flat, Setup2 turned 90° about X (or Y) with "What Setup1 leaves behind" simulates, judges gouges and feeds rest/judged stock from the carried body; a pinning test carries a faced plate side-on and checks its volume and verdict.

labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
From the same Makera Z1 user report (2026-11-11). Makera machines cool with **air, M7**. The user built a Z1 machine file in the editor and tried to add M7 air cooling: **"this was ignored when I saved the profile"**. They asked to be able to:
- disable the default (flood) cooling in the editor and swap it for air; or
- keep both in the profile and choose one per operation.

**What we know from the code (main):**
- A new machine draft is seeded with `"coolants": [{ "name": "Flood", "mCode": "M8" }]` (`crates/app/src/machine/draft.rs:91`).
- `add_coolant` adds a name with **no code** (`draft.rs:147-165`). A coolant whose code is never filled in may then be skipped or dropped. That's likely the "ignored on save".
- `carvera.cps` `coolantCode()` returns the **first `Flood` entry**, else the first entry with a code. So a profile still holding the seeded Flood M8 posts **M8**, even after an Air M7 is added. On a Makera that's the wrong M-code: M8 isn't the air blast.
- Operations choose `CoolantMode` Off / Flood / Mist / Through tool (`crates/post/src/post/coolant.rs`). There's no **Air** mode, and Flood is the silent default, so an op can't ask for "air" by name. The generic posts look the word up in the machine's list and refuse by name when it's missing.

**Fix (sketch; the worker decides the details and records them):**
1. **The editor** can remove or replace the seeded Flood entry, and an added coolant gets its code entered before it's saved. A save never silently drops a coolant; it's refused by name if one is incomplete.
2. **An `Air` coolant mode** (or "air blast", M7 on Makera), selectable per operation, which the posts resolve from the machine's list like Mist.
3. **A machine-level default coolant**, so a machine whose only coolant is air defaults new operations to Air, not Flood.
4. **`carvera.cps`** posts the coolant the operation asked for, not "first Flood". If the machine has no matching entry, it's a named refusal, never a wrong M-code.

Effort: high: it changes posted G-code (safety floor).

**Done means:**
- a machine file with only Air M7 posts M7/M9 for a default operation;
- a profile edited in the GUI keeps its Air M7 after save and reload;
- an operation asking for a coolant the machine lacks is refused by name;
- all pinned.

title: Simulation and reach laws: read a tool's drawn cutter/neck outline (a necked tool reaches deeper than its shank cylinder)

labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while working #93 (slice 2: the drawn cutter, neck and shank in the tool editor).

What happens: a milling tool's own shape can now be drawn as a spun half-outline (`schema::ToolCutter`, set by `SetToolCutter`, `camcraft_tools::cutter_profile`). By design it is display only: the generators, the stock simulation and the reach / shank / holder laws keep reading the tool's numbers (`diameter`, `flute_len`, `shank_d`, `shank_len`). The drawn outline is held to agree with those numbers (`cutter_profile::check`: exact diameter within the flutes, flute + shank length, never wider than the stated shank above the flutes), so the numbers are always the conservative envelope - but a necked tool (a reduced neck under the flutes, the whole point of buying one) is still judged as the full shank cylinder, so reach checks over-report and refuse cuts the real tool makes.

What should: the simulation's tool body and the reach laws may read the drawn outline where it is narrower than the numbers' cylinder, never where it would be wider - one source for the judged envelope, the same way the drawn holder feeds `tool_body` / the band stack.

Evidence: `crates/app/src/tool_cutter.rs` (reader/writer), `crates/tools/src/cutter_profile.rs` (agreement law); the judged envelope lives in `tool_body` / `HolderStack` and (open) PR #837 / #843 `sim_tool_body`, band stack - this must build on those once merged, not beside them.

Done means: a tool with a drawn neck narrower than its shank is judged at the neck in the reach / shank laws and drawn so by the simulation; a tool with no drawn cutter judges bit-identically to today; pinned by tests both ways.

Part of #93 (follow-up, out of its scope: "feeding the profile into the stock simulation and collision laws").

title: adaptive growth: the overload fallback picks the largest step on truncated readings and walks it far past the bound

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
What happens: `Planner::step_search` (crates/motion/src/machining2d/adaptive/grow.rs) tries up to 7 growth steps with `walk_until(.., limit = bound)`, which stops at the FIRST reading past the bound. When no step holds, the fallback keeps "the least overload" from those truncated readings. Where the overload sits before the g-dependent front (it does not grow with the step), every try reads the same, the tie goes to the first (largest) step, and that step is then walked whole - far past the reading it was chosen on.

Evidence (release, `HSM_ONE=island hsm_one`, island 60x40/12x12, on d1920031 with the #844 compile break stubbed locally and the growth budget lifted to reach the growth): round the island's NE corner, revs 153-159 read the same first exceedance at every step from 1.88 down to 0.088 mm (e.g. rev 159: 59.5 deg x7), the largest step was kept and walked whole at 57.5 -> 125 deg (79.4 % D at (43.66, 25.81)). This is the 125 deg / 176 breaks round 9 of #7 blamed on the spiral's geometry.

Held fix: branch `issue/7-r10-corner-reading`, e4039ef0 - re-walk each tried step whole and keep the least. Island readings with it: every overloaded revolution reads <= 55 deg (bound ~47.5; worst now at the SW wall, (17.58, 6.01)), the NE-corner overloads are gone. Cost: the growth work on the island doubles (61,971 r, vs ~31,000 before, vs the #13 `WORK_MAX` 30,000), because the smaller steps take more revolutions, and each overloaded revolution adds up to 7 whole walks.

Done means: the fallback chooses the least overload by whole readings (a pinning test where the truncated reading ties and the whole reading does not), with the #13 growth budget kept honest (either the extra walks are not charged as growth work, the re-walk is bounded, or WORK_MAX is recalibrated on the fixtures with the band refusal re-timed); goldens that move are listed.

Found while working #7 (round 10). Part of the #7 picture, but a defect on any growth plan with an overloaded revolution.

body:
Found while working #835 (PR stacked on #837).

**What happens.** #835 moves the verdict laws that read the tool's stack above the shank - reach (c), the mid-turn sweep (c3), the solid law (b2), the containment solid law, posed rapids and the rotary field law - onto the body's band stack (`Cutter::body`, `tool_body::stack`), the shape the simulation draws. Three laws still read one holder cylinder by construction and so judge a modelled tool body (#368 mesh, #93 drawn profile) by the cylinder enclosing it:

- `crates/app/src/operation/drill_reach.rs` - the axial holder-face law and `cross_holder` (one disc / tube at `holder_d`, from the shank top);
- `crates/app/src/operation/cross_part.rs` - `part_clear` builds `Cutter::of(tool)` without the body;
- `crates/app/src/operation/probe_op.rs` - `stylus_cutter` folds stem and holder into one band.

They over-report only (never smaller than the body), and since #835 their refusals / the probe path say so by name ("the tool body is judged here by the cylinder enclosing it, Ø..."). But a stepped body (narrow nose under a wide flange) can still be refused for a flange that never reaches the stock.

**Expected.** Each reads the band stack: drill reach checks each band's face disc against the material over that band's radius; cross_part takes the body-carrying cutter; the stylus is rebuilt as stem + the body's bands.

Evidence: `docs/decisions/835-reach-reads-band-stack.md` (kept-cylinder list), `operation::body_judged`.

Done means: those three laws read the same band stack the simulation draws, with a pinning test per law for a stepped body whose nose clears and whose flange does not reach, and the enclosure wording is dropped from them.

Part of #743.

title: Synthetos TinyG post processor (3-axis mill)

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
### What are you trying to do

Post 3-axis milling programs for machines running [Synthetos TinyG](https://github.com/synthetos/TinyG) (the TinyG v8 board, ATxmega192A3), the other grbl-family hobby controller. CamCraft has no TinyG post; #710's grblHAL post is the closest, but TinyG understands a smaller set again: no canned cycles at all (G81-G89 are rejected), no G41/G42, no G84, `M6` only records the tool, tool numbers stop at 31, and the serial input acts on `!`, `~` and `%` wherever they stand in a line.

The firmware's `edge-next` branch (build 450.03) is what I maintain and test on real boards, so posted programs can be checked against its own parser and planner off the board, and on a board after that.

### How you imagine it working

A new `assets/posts/tinyg.cps` (3-axis mill), structured like `grblhal.cps` and specced from TinyG's public wiki ("Gcode Support", "Homing and Limits", "Flow Control and Footers", "Inch and Millimeter Units Mode") and the LinuxCNC G-code reference TinyG states it follows (behaviour only; the firmware source is GPL and is not read for this), plus a generic `assets/machines/tinyg-3axis.mch`.

What the post respects (each checked against the wiki and by replaying the output through the edge-next parser and planner):
- **Drilling as plain moves**: a CYCLE record writes nothing; the hole's expanded chain posts, with the dwell as `G4 P<seconds>` at the hole bottom. Tapping is refused by name (no G84, no spindle sync).
- **Tool change**: Z lift, then `T<n> M6` alone on its line, then `M0` on the next - M6 moves nothing on TinyG, so the stop is the operator's change. Tools T1-T31; a larger number is refused by name.
- **Header `G21|G20 G17 G90 G91.1 G94 G64`**: the words M30 does not reset on TinyG. No `%`, O word or N numbers; no tool length word (G43.1/G49 belong to the operator or sender, as #710 decided for grblHAL).
- **Z lift as grblHAL's**: `G53 G0 Z<safe_retract>` only when the machine file states it; otherwise the work-offset clearance, refused by name when unknown or not above the stock. No G28/G30.
- **Comments** drop `!` (feed hold), `~` (cycle start), `%` (queue flush) and the other characters the serial input acts on; lines stay under 191 bytes.
- Refused by name: control/wear compensation, going home, tilted moves; probing is refused by the engine (no parameters or expressions on TinyG).

**Done means:** `tinyg.cps` and the machine file ship in `assets/`; the post is in the conformance list (tap refused), `EXTENSIONS` and the cross-post tests like `grblhal`; a `tinyg_post` test and goldens under `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/tinyg/` cover contour, pocket, face, slot, trace, drill, peck and tool change; every golden replays through the edge-next firmware's parser and planner with no refused line.

Related: #710 (grblHAL post; this stacks on #715, which it extends the same lists as), #714.

Filed from a fork, which cannot set labels. Suggested labels: enhancement, P2, area:post.

Found in the high-tier review of PR #815 (#813): https://github.com/NeoTech/Camcraft/pull/815#pullrequestreview-5856868422

**The gap:**
- A work-turning rotary about **Y** (a table B: vector `[0,1,0]`, or none and named B) is treated as off X. It gets **no swing check, no refusal and no load note**, so a `G0 B..` index could swing the work into the retracted tool unjudged.
- It's the same risk as the A case (#804/#810, #813/#815): a vertical tool tip at height h is at least h from any horizontal line through the WCS origin.
- A rotary named A whose *stated* vector is off X falls through the same way.
- **C is safe:** turning about a vertical line keeps every point's height.

**Today it's latent:** no shipped machine has a work-turning B (millturn's C carries the head), and nothing judged any swing before #804.

**Expected:**
- Generalise `rotary_line` and the swept radius in `crates/app/src/posting_index_swing.rs` to any work-turning rotary about a HORIZONTAL line through the WCS origin.
- Refuse by name when `nose_to_axis` is unstated, exactly as for A.
- Extend the load note (`project/swing_note.rs`) to those rotaries too.

Effort: high (a post-gate safety law).

**Done means:** a table-B machine (a test `.mch`) gets the same index-swing judgement as the microARC A, with refusal and clear pins, and a horizontal-line A with an off-X vector is judged. Pinned, and a revert check shows each pin fails.

title: Holder library follow-ups: confirm the flare envelope against a measured holder, re-seed the projection, no silent ER fallback

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:sim
labels.description: Stock simulation and verification

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P8
labels.description: Larger idea needing design or research before code

body:
Follow-ups from the high-tier review of PR #805 (#792), building on PR #800 (#793).

1. **The flare envelope only covers abrupt flares.** The body-to-flange envelope is a 45° cone ending at the flange front. It covers real flares at least that abrupt. A *gentler* flare (e.g. 1 radial mm per 2-3 axial mm) stands outside the cone near its foot, and the band reading only partly offsets that.
   - Fix the wording in `docs/decisions/792-er-collets.md`: it currently says "no steeper than 45 degrees" and should say "no more gradual than 45°".
   - **Decide the envelope after the user's hand measurement** of their BT30 ER20 holder. If a real flare is gentler, widen the envelope (a shallower cone, or a full-flange cylinder down to the nut top), so the model never under-reports the steel.
2. **The projection can go stale:** the picker seeds it at pick time (`crates/ui/src/state_tool_profile.rs:186-192`). If the tool's lengths are then edited and applied before "Apply holder", the holder lands higher than the steel. Re-seed it on a tool change, or flag the mismatch.
3. In `holder_library.rs:310-312`, the `sizes` closure's `unwrap_or(0)` silently falls back to ER11 for an unknown size name. Return a named error instead, and add an entry-count-per-taper test.

Effort: high (holder geometry feeds the collision checks).

**Done means:**
- The decision wording is corrected.
- The envelope is confirmed or widened from the measured holder.
- The projection re-seeds.
- No silent fallback remains.
- Each item is pinned.

body:
# Part alignment from two perpendicular edge picks: the picks define the full 3D frame

## What

The axis-pick panel (Setup > align) refuses an out-of-plane pick: "the
+Y pick runs (nearly) along the work plane's normal (Z)". But two
perpendicular picks — an edge for +X, an edge for +Y — already define a
complete 3D frame: the +X pick's direction maps to world +X, the +Y
pick's to world +Y, and Z+ follows by the right-hand rule (the user's
rule: the directions decide where Z+ points). Today's `turn_in_plane`
(`app/src/pick/axis.rs`) only spins about the work plane's normal and
throws that information away.

## The law (from the discussion with the user)

- Pick two lines (edges or two-point picks) that run across each
  other: the +X pick's direction maps to world +X, the +Y pick's to
  world +Y, and the part's Z+ lands where the right-hand rule puts it
  (R(d_x) x R(d_y) = +Z).
- The pivot is the parts' centre (the part stays on its spot of the
  table) — the ORIGIN question is deliberately out of scope here: the
  work offset is placed separately, as it is today.
- Nearly-perpendicular picks: the primary axis lands exactly, the
  secondary is orthogonalized against it; picks that run (nearly)
  along each other refuse by name (no frame can be read from them).
- Flip flags keep their meaning (a reversed edge flips its direction).
- The landing is proven before the command stores anything (the
  primary runs along its axis, the secondary within the skew it came
  with, the frame right-handed) — never a silently wrong frame.

## Scope

- `pick/axis.rs`: `align_from_axes(world, setup, axes)` — the general
  construction, which subsumes the in-plane turn for in-plane picks.
- `commands/setup_align.rs`: the `AlignPartToSetup` constructor for it.
- The UI call site (`ui/src/state.rs`, the axis-pick panel's apply)
  switches from `turn_in_plane` to the general path — the same panel,
  the same picks, now with the full meaning.
- `turn_in_plane` stays for its in-plane callers; the general path must
  reproduce its results for in-plane picks (subsumption, pinned
  numerically).

## Done means

- The user's exact case aligns: a part whose +Y edge runs along world
  (0, 0, -1) and +X edge along (-1, 0, 0) lands with +Y along +Y, +X
  along +X and the cross-normal up — one pick round, no plane-first
  step.
- In-plane picks behave exactly as `turn_in_plane` did (existing suites
  green: turn_pivot, plane_align, the setup axis tests).
- Numeric tests: out-of-plane perpendicular picks, subsumption for
  in-plane picks, near-perpendicular skew, parallel picks refused by
  name, flips honored, undo restores.

body:
# One machining-frame seam: OpFrame composes part_alignment and TiltedFrame

## What

The part-alignment machinery (#326) and the per-operation tilt frame (the
3+2 index, M5.1 B) both exist and both work — but only separately.
`setup_align::generation_problem` allows generation in an aligned setup for
exactly four kinds (Face, 2D Contour, 2D Pocket, 2D Adaptive), and tilt
inside an aligned setup is refused outright. Every other planar kind,
picks, and area controls are refused by name. The refusals are a
verification gap, not a mathematical one: the two mechanisms compose as
plain function composition.

This issue builds ONE seam — `OpFrame`, `crates/app/src/operation/frame.rs`
— that composes the two existing mechanisms and becomes the single door
the generators' world reads go through. No generator rewrites: the motion
generators take data (facets, regions, heights); only the app read/wrap
seam moves.

## The frame contract

Coordinate systems:

- **D** — document frame (as modelled). Part entities carry their
  `Location` in D.
- **S** — setup frame: the table frame, also the world the CL stream and
  the post speak. Stock, WCS and fixtures are setup FURNITURE — stored in
  S already (#326's law; their world reads are correct and stay untouched).
- **L** — local machining frame: XY = the cutting plane, +Z = the tool
  axis. Exists only when the op tilts.

Point maps (right-to-left application, the `setup_align::compose`
convention):

- D → S: `A` = the setup's `part_alignment`, baked into part geometry
  reads (`facets_in` and siblings). Never inverted — the CL never maps
  back to D.
- S → L: `T` = `TiltedFrame` from `op.params.tilt()` (`to_local`), applied
  AFTER the alignment read: `p_L = T(A(p_D))`.
- L → S (CL out): `T.to_world`, the tilt's inverse. The whole CL stream
  wraps through `TiltedFrame::world_path`; identity when no tilt exists.

Layers stay separate (never a fourth):

1. part_alignment — setup, physical (how the part is clamped)
2. WCS — program zero (translation today)
3. operation tool orientation — the `Tilt` param

Machine-side relations remain derived internal transforms composed from
these; no user-facing SCS, no second offset frame.

## Design conditions (from the plan review)

1. **Heights and bounding boxes resolve against fully transformed
   geometry** (local bounds of `T(A(f))`), never a bare `z − origin.z`
   shift — a Z shift is not generally correct for an arbitrarily tilted
   plane. `OpFrame`'s height and AABB reads implement this from day one.
2. **Machine capability gates are preserved and pinned by tests**: a
   tilted orientation never silently posts as plain XYZ when the machine
   cannot reach it. The post's tilted-record refusals (non-RTCP, no
   rotary) keep their verdicts.
3. **Stepwise integration**: Phase 1 wires the seam behind the four
   currently-supported kinds, byte-identical. Refusals lift only as their
   numeric tests land: picks in aligned setups next, then further 2D/3D
   families, alignment × tilt last.

## Phases

- **Phase 1 (first branch)**: `OpFrame` + the four kinds through it,
  behavior byte-identical; the seam's math pinned by unit tests (identity,
  90°/180° alignment, alignment × tilt composition, transformed picks,
  local heights on tilted planes, AABBs under arbitrary rotation, CL
  back-transform, tool direction, capability gates, byte-identity).
- **Phase 2**: the selection walk reads picked parts through the seam
  (`facets_in`); picks in aligned setups verified. Tilt × picks stays
  refused.
- **Phase 3**: `verified_kind` extended kind by kind (whole-model 3D
  kinds first), each with a pinned numeric test; area controls; then tilt
  × alignment.
- **Phase 4**: re-evaluate #760 (rotated-offset carry) on top of the
  unified seam — normal 3-axis work needs alignment coverage, not offset
  rotation.

## Done means (Phase 1)

- `crates/app/src/operation/frame.rs` exists with the contract above;
  `collect_job` reads geometry/heights for the four kinds through it.
- The mandatory test list above is green.
- Existing aligned-setup tests (#326's) and goldens pass unchanged —
  byte-identical output.
- No refusal lifted, no post change, no generator change.

Related: #326 (part alignment), #316 (setup-to-setup transform), #315
(rotation refusal at the post), #760 (rotated-offset carry — re-evaluated
in phase 4, untouched by this issue's branches).

body:
**What happens**

The 3-2-1 alignment (#187) and `SetWcsOrigin` can set a rotated work offset, and the viewport shows the rotated frame — but nothing downstream machines in it:

- Toolpaths generate in world axes; only the offset's translation (`wcs_context` → `OriginX/Y/Z`) reaches the record stream (`posting_wcs_rotation.rs`).
- Heights / machining planes stay world-Z.
- The post refuses a rotated offset by name (#315, shipped in v0.15.0) — correct and safe, but by then the user has built a state the whole page presented as valid: the display shows a frame the CAM does not machine.

User-reported on main 5fd45923: align a setup's WCS with 3-2-1 on a turned part → the WCS is right in the display, toolpath and machining plane do not follow. Not yet pinned by a test.

**Fix (step 3 of #315, owed)**

Carry the rotation end-to-end, as a user parameter with a default:

- generation and heights compute in the offset's frame, so toolpath and machining planes follow the alignment, and
- the post either bakes rotated coordinates into the program or emits the control's own rotation where the machine declares it (Fanuc G68 / G68.2, Siemens CYCLE800 / ROT, Heidenhain PLANE / CYCL 10 — public control documentation only; a G54 register is translation only on every control).

Interim, if the full carry is not taken at once: the 3-2-1 flow should say at alignment time that a rotated offset will not post (the refusal currently arrives only at the post gate), or steer to part alignment (#330, #746).

**Done means**

A part aligned with a rotated work offset machines in that frame: toolpath, height planes and posted program all carry the same rotation, pinned against a hand-computed program — or the alignment refuses with a clear message before any toolpath exists. Never a display that shows a frame nothing machines.

**Related**: #315 (the shipped refusal), #187 (3-2-1 alignment), #330 / #746 (part alignment, the alternative path), #701 (will create rotated offsets from feature roles and needs this to machine them).

body:
Requested by the maintainer; sibling of #743 (tool and holder bodies as spun profiles).

## Two fixture variants
A fixture is one of:
- **Spun body** (turning: chucks, jaws, collets, faceplates): a half-profile on a centreline, revolved about the spindle axis. The same representation as #743's tool and holder bodies, and the same profile code.
- **Extruded profile** (milling: vises, jaws, parallels, step blocks): a closed 2D profile and an extrusion depth (along a chosen axis), placed in the setup.

## Import paths
- **From DXF.** A spun fixture is a centreline plus a half-profile, like #743. An extruded fixture is a closed profile plus the extrusion depth (entered on import, or from a DXF annotation/layer if present). Editable afterwards the way the half-profile is.
- **From STEP.** Imported as a solid and **kept and saved as STEP** in the fixture library (not converted to a profile): the fixture case keeps the vendor solid. A spun or extruded profile can optionally be derived from it, but the STEP stays the source.
- DXF read/write is shared with #743 (our own, from the published DXF reference: `LINE`, `ARC`, `LWPOLYLINE`, layers), with named refusals for unsupported entities and open or self-crossing profiles.

## Collision and simulation
- Spun and extruded fixtures are meshed for the fixture laws and the simulation from their exact profiles, so a profile edit changes what is checked and drawn.
- A STEP fixture keeps today's mesh path.

## Related
- #743: tool and holder bodies as spun profiles (shares the profile/DXF code).
- #339: handle fixtures and vises (umbrella); #561/#566 (locate the part in a fixture); the fixture library (`fixture_library`, #339); #723 (fixture_library test on Windows).

## Done means
- A spun fixture imports from a DXF half-profile and an extruded fixture from a DXF closed profile plus a depth. Both are tested: the meshed body matches the profile, and malformed input gives a named error, not a panic.
- A STEP fixture imports, saves to the fixture library as STEP, and re-inserts unchanged (test).
- The fixture laws and the simulation use the profile-built bodies (existing fixture suites pass; a new test checks a vise jaw built from a profile is hit by a rapid through it).

body:
Requested by the maintainer.

## 1. Simulation shows the tool and holder as spun profiles
While simulating, draw the **tool and its holder as revolved bodies**: the half-profile spun about the spindle axis, at the tool's position and orientation each frame. Today's simulation doesn't show them as solids. Use the same profile the collision laws judge (the revolved envelope, #368), so what you see is what is checked.

## 2. Imported tool bodies and holders become an editable half-profile
When a tool body or holder is imported as **STEP**, convert it to a **2D half-profile on a centreline** (the meridian of the revolved envelope: radius against height along the tool axis). Store it as a **DXF**, with the centreline as its own entity/layer, so the profile can be edited (in the spun-profile editor, #93) and re-exported.

- Only the half-profile is editable, and the body is always its revolution about the centreline.
- Conversion should be conservative: the profile is the outer envelope (max radius at each height), never smaller than the solid, so collision checks stay safe. Non-revolved features (flats, coolant holes, the holder's drive slots) are enveloped, never cut away. Say so in the UI.
- Refuse by name when the STEP body has no clear axis (axis detection/alignment: #370) instead of guessing one.
- A tool/holder can also be **imported directly as a DXF half-profile** (a centreline plus an open profile on one side of it).
- DXF read/write is our own, written from the published DXF reference (entities `LINE`, `ARC`, `LWPOLYLINE`, layers). The minimum needed is lines and arcs, with a named refusal for anything else (splines, unclosed profiles that cross the centreline).

## Related
- #93 spun (revolved-profile) design editor for tool and holder shapes: the editor for these profiles.
- #361 import vendor STEP tool models; #368 a vendor holder judged by its revolved envelope (closed); #370 align a vendor STEP by its tool coordinate systems; #371 pick tip and axis on an imported body (closed).
- Fixtures get the same treatment in a sibling issue.

## Done means
- The simulation draws the tool and holder as revolved solids from their profiles (structural/paint assertion where possible, hand-tested by the maintainer; no snapshot PNG changes).
- Importing a STEP holder produces a DXF half-profile with a centreline, and the envelope encloses the original solid (a test samples the STEP mesh and checks every point lies inside the revolved profile).
- A DXF half-profile imports as a tool/holder body; malformed DXF (no centreline, spline, crossing profile) is a named error in a test, never a panic.
- Round trip: STEP → DXF → body → DXF is stable within tolerance.

body:
## What's wrong

`docs/decisions/578-units-in-errors.md` split the millimeter-speaking strings into tiers and lensed the transient ones (#590). The tier it listed under **Considered and dropped** is still open, and it is the tier a user actually reads when an operation refuses:

> Generator refusals in `operation/circle_fit` and the `operation::*` generate paths, and the pure-crate `Display` refusals (`tools`: `spun`, `holder_profile`, `lathe_holder`, `lathe_insert_zone`; `motion`: `descent`, `probing`): these live below the app - pure functions and pure-crate types with no world and no unit in scope. Threading a `Unit` through those APIs for a handful of refusal sentences is a wide signature change with no lens to hang it on.

So in an inch document the fields all read inches and the refusal banner still says millimeters. It is worse than a missing suffix: several sentences *hardcode the word* "mm", so the text is not merely unit-blind, it is wrong.

## Where

The lens is `app::units::of(world)` over the pure formatters in `geometry::units` (`len`, `feed`, `area`, `vol`). Every site below builds its sentence without one:

**App generate paths** (`crates/app/src/operation/`)

| site | sentence |
| --- | --- |
| `material.rs:221`, `:224` | `no material at z = {z:.3}` - no unit at all |
| `area.rs:100`, `:193` | `the part fills the whole selection at Z {z:.3}` |
| `drill_reach.rs:73` | `is {depth:.3} mm deep from the stock surface; tool {name}'s flute reaches {flute:.3} mm` |
| `drill_reach.rs:201-204` | `cycle at ({:.3}, {:.3}) is {depth:.3} mm deep ... past tool {name}'s {flute:.3} mm flute, and its shank dia. {shank_d:.3} does not fit the dia. {} hole` |
| `circle_fit.rs:67` | `deviation {dev:.3} mm at ({:.3}, {:.3})` |
| `contour_open.rs:238-240` | `the open boundary's offset of {d:.3} mm folds onto itself` |
| `cross_stock.rs:284-287` | `cross-drill rapid {i} stops {got:.3} mm out along its hole's line ... ({need:.3} mm)` |

**Pure-crate refusals**

| site | sentence |
| --- | --- |
| `motion/src/machining2d/face.rs:329` | `{what} {step} mm over {span:.3} mm needs more than {MAX_PASSES} passes` |
| `motion/src/drilling/axial.rs:119` | `the drill is {tool_d} mm across, the bore at ({}, {}) is modeled {} mm` |
| `motion/src/finishing3d/params.rs:267` | `3D finish {name} {s} mm reaches the scallop ceiling: passes a ball diameter ({d} mm) apart` |
| `tools/src/spun.rs:79`, `:90` | `shorter than {MIN_SEGMENT} mm`, `({MAX_BODY_RADIUS} mm from the axis, {MAX_BODY_HEIGHT} mm long)` |
| `tools/src/holder_profile.rs:94` | `larger than any tool a spindle carries (500 mm from the axis, 2000 mm long)` |
| `tools/src/lathe_holder.rs:95-97` | `farther than 2000 mm from its tip`, `more than 50.8 mm from the lathe body`, `within 25.4 mm of it` |
| `tools/src/lathe_insert_zone.rs:48` | `reaches {reach:.3} mm from the tip along {axis}, past the {cap:.3} mm one insert can` |
| `motion`: `machining2d/descent`, `machining3d/descent`, `probing` | same shape, named by the decision doc |

## Why it matters

AGENTS.md treats a refusal as data the user acts on, and #261 part 2 already went out of its way to make refusals *locatable* rather than readable as coordinates. A refusal in the wrong units is the same failure from the other side: the sentence tells an inch user to "raise the clearance" against a number that is 25.4x off from what every field on their screen shows.

## Two ways to fix it, and why they are cheaper than they look

1. **Structured refusals** - store the numbers, format at display, the way `sim::verify::Warning` already does. This is the pattern the decision doc already picked for tier 2, so it lands once and covers both tiers' persisted/transient split.
2. **An additive `Unit` argument** on the pure-crate formatters - the decision doc's own closing line: "the pure-crate Displays want a `Unit` argument, additive once anyone wants it."

Neither is as wide as the doc feared, because `GenError` already carries structured data through a frame boundary: `GenError::At { msg, at }` stores a `Point3` and `GenError::map_location` maps it to world *before the UI sees it* (`motion/src/machining2d/gen_error.rs`). A refusal that carries `{ depth_mm, flute_mm }` and formats at display time rides that same already-solved rail, and the app's `run_job` is already the place that knows the world's unit.

The `mm`-hardcoded sentences are the part worth fixing first regardless of which shape is chosen: they can move to `units::len`-style formatting at display time without any new type.

## Pinning it

The `len`/`feed`/`area` law (mm mode byte-identical, inches = the mm precision plus extra decimals) makes this pin-testable the way #590 pinned the gouge clause. `blind_floor::the_gouge_clause_speaks_the_document_s_units` is the template: same world, inch lens, assert the sentence divides by 25.4, says "in", and never says "mm"; and an untouched mm pin proving the mm strings did not move.

One caveat for whoever takes it: the pure-crate refusals that quote *constants* rather than user numbers (`spun`'s `MIN_SEGMENT`, `holder_profile`'s 500/2000 mm spindle ceilings, `lathe_holder`'s 25.4/50.8 mm insert limits) are the MACHINE's/catalog's numbers, not the document's, and the decision doc already ruled that class separate ("the `.mch` grammar has its own unit story"). This issue is about the sentences quoting numbers the user typed into fields that already ride the lens.

title: WCS page: anchor on a circle's centre (pick a circular edge), as a reusable pick, and tidy the page layout

body:
Reported by the maintainer while hand-testing the WCS page (screenshot in chat: X/Y/Z origin, Tilt/Turn fields, quarter-turn buttons, "Anchor on" Stock box with Bottom/Middle/Top, "Pick markers in viewport", and the NW…SE grid).

## 1. Anchor on the centre of a circle

Today the WCS can be anchored on a grid point of the stock box or the model's bounds (NW…SE × Bottom/Middle/Top, or picked markers). Add **anchoring on the centre of a circle**, e.g. a hole or a boss: pick a circular (or arc) edge and the WCS origin goes to its centre (the circle's centre point, at the edge's height; the circle's axis is available for later use).

- **Reusable.** Build "circle centre from a picked edge" as a shared pick primitive in the app layer, next to the pick graph (#692 / `pick`), not inside the WCS page. Other tools will reuse it: setup alignment (#738), WCS roles (#701), probing, hole features. It should take an edge pick and return the centre, axis and radius, or a named refusal when the edge isn't circular within tolerance (a straight edge, a spline, an open polyline that doesn't fit a circle). Never return a guessed centre.
- **On the page:** a separate group under "Anchor on", cleanly separated from the stock-box/model grid. For example an "Anchor on: Stock box / Model / **Circle centre**" choice, where Circle centre shows "Pick a circular edge" plus the picked result ("Circle Ø 8.00 mm, centre (x, y, z)").
- **Undoable command** like the other WCS edits, with its MCP tool (AGENTS.md "Commands ship with an MCP tool"), or a filed `MCP: ...` follow-up.

## 2. Layout: the page is cluttered

- **Value fields:** label and input on **one row**, with the inputs aligned in a column (a two-column grid: "X origin [ 0.0 mm ]"). Today each input drops below its label.
- **Quarter-turn buttons** (Turn X+ … Turn Z-, Level, Set Origin): same size, filling the pane's width in an even grid, rather than leaving a ragged right edge.
- **Anchor grid** (NW N NE / W [C] E / SW S SE): equal-size buttons, a bit larger, centred or filling the pane's width, so it reads as a 3×3 compass.
- Group the page into clear sections (Origin and orientation · Quarter turns · Anchor on), so the circle-centre option sits in its own group.

## Related
- #692: one pick rule and pick API (circle-centre builds on its feature edges).
- #701: set the WCS from picked features with roles.
- #738: setup-page alignment and pick visibility (reuses the circle-centre pick).

## Done means
- Picking a circular edge on the WCS page sets the origin to the circle's centre. Pinned by an app test on a mesh with a drilled hole, comparing the centre to the true one within tolerance, plus a test that a straight edge is refused by name, plus undo restoring the previous origin.
- The circle-centre function lives in a shared module with its own tests and is called from the WCS page, not written inside it.
- The layout changes are checked by the structural assertions (labels and fields on one row, buttons present and enabled), with no snapshot PNG changes in the PR.
- An MCP tool for the new anchor exists, or a follow-up issue is filed.

title: Setup page alignment: one clear flow, moves apply to the body as it is, and picks you can actually see

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:ui
labels.description: User interface and picking

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Reported by the maintainer while hand-testing the setup page's part alignment (screenshot of the Setups page attached in chat: Part alignment dropdown at the top, then "Lay on a plane - pick a face", "pick three points", "Axes in the plane - pick an edge or two points").

## What's wrong

1. **The "Part alignment" control at the top overrides the pickers.** The dropdown and the Turn X/Y/Z + about + Apply row sit above the face, three-point and edge/two-point pickers, and applying one wipes out what the others did. It's unclear which one is in charge. The page should read as one flow, where the pickers are the way to align and the preset/turn row doesn't silently override them (or is clearly a separate "start from a preset" step).
2. **Each pick-driven move resets the part and then moves it.** Laying on a face, on three points or applying axes first returns the body to its import pose and then applies only the new transform. Expected: each move applies **to the body as it is now** (incremental, composed with what was done before), and undo steps back one move at a time.
3. **Pick status shows internal ids.** "Face 0xccc7c…" (the welded-face id) means nothing to a user. Show the count and the kind: "1 face selected", "2 points selected", "1 edge selected".
4. **Picked geometry is hard to see.**
   - **Faces:** only the outline is drawn in purple. Fill the whole picked face with the pick colour (semi-transparent), so it's obvious which face it is.
   - **Vertices / points:** draw them as round, visible markers (filled discs, somewhat transparent is fine), not a speck.
   - **Edges:** the picked edge line is so thin it barely shows against the grey part. Draw it noticeably thicker (bold).

## Related
- #692 (one picking rule for the whole app: what is pickable). This issue is about how picks are *shown* and how the alignment page *applies* them.
- #330, #555, #557, #606 (lay on a face, three-point plane, axes by edge/two points, align about the WCS origin): the features this page combines.
- #701 (WCS from picked features with roles).

## Done means
- Applying a face, three-point or axis alignment moves the part from its current pose; a pinning test applies two alignments in a row and checks the second composes on the first, and undo restores each step.
- The top "Part alignment" preset/turn row no longer silently discards a picker's result (pinned by a test, or the page is restructured so the two can't conflict); the flow is described in the page's tooltips.
- Pick status reads "N face(s)/edge(s)/point(s) selected", with no internal ids (structural test).
- Picked faces are filled with the pick colour, picked points are round markers, and picked edges are drawn bold. Checked by the structural/paint assertions where they can be, hand-tested by the maintainer otherwise (no snapshot PNG changes in the PR).

title: MCP: edit and delete a document tool (ChangeTool, DeleteTool)

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server and agent tooling (crates/app/src/mcp, camcraft-mcp skill)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
**What's missing:** a document tool can be added over MCP (`add_tool`), but it can't be edited or deleted. The tool editor's commands are `ChangeTool` (replace the definition, so ops on the tool turn stale) and `DeleteTool` (remove it; undo restores its number and body), both in `crates/app/src/commands/tool.rs`. A headless agent that needs a longer stickout, a different flute count or another rpm has to add a second tool under a new name and re-point every op with `set_tool`. A tool added by mistake can only go by `undo`.

**Neighbour that works:** `edit_operation { name, params }` applies a JSON merge patch over an op's fields, refuses an unknown field by name, and runs `EditOperationParams` (`crates/app/src/mcp/edit.rs`).

**Done means:**
- `edit_tool { name, definition }` applies a JSON merge patch over the tool's `get_job` definition, refuses an unknown field by name, and runs `ChangeTool` through `env.history`, one undo step. The command's own refusals come back as tool errors: non-finite or non-positive numbers, a retype the tool law refuses for an op using the tool, a body that no longer fits.
- `delete_tool { name }` runs `DeleteTool`, one undo step. The reply names any operations that still use the tool.
- In-process JSON-RPC tests pin both: an edit makes the op stale, undo restores it, and the refusals are named. They also cover what verify and post do once a used tool is gone.

**What's missing:** the MCP server can add and activate setups (`add_setup`, `activate_setup`), but it can't move an operation into another setup or delete a setup. Both are app commands the GUI uses: `SetOperationSetup` (`crates/app/src/commands/setup.rs`) and `DeleteSetup` (`crates/app/src/commands/setup_delete.rs`). A headless agent that put an op in the wrong setup, or added one setup too many, can only `undo` back to that point and redo the work after it.

**Neighbour that works:** `add_setup` / `activate_setup` (`crates/app/src/mcp/setup_tools.rs`) run `CreateSetup` / `ActivateSetup` through the History.

`DeleteSetup` already refuses a setup that still machines operations, with `'<op>' machines in '<setup>' - move or delete it first`. Over MCP, half of that advice has no tool to follow it.

**Done means:**
- `set_operation_setup { operation, setup }` runs `SetOperationSetup` through `env.history`. `setup` is a declared setup, or null for the implicit first position. The command keeps the stamp, so the op reads `ok` or `stale` by the staleness law.
- `delete_setup { name }` runs `DeleteSetup`. It takes the setup's private furniture with it, and one undo restores them.
- Both return what changed. The commands' refusals come back as tool errors: an unknown op or setup, a move to where the op already is, a setup an op still machines in, and a setup another one is placed relative to.
- In-process JSON-RPC tests pin it: moving an op between two setups, deleting the emptied setup, undo and redo, and the refusals.

title: Machines: Sienci AltMill (2×4, 4×4, 4×8) on the SLB-EXT, posting through the grblHAL post

labels.name: claimed
labels.description: An agent is working on this - see the claim comment

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P6
labels.description: Accepted enhancement, not scheduled

body:
Add machine definitions, and the post they need, for Sienci Labs' AltMill CNC routers, driven by the SLB-EXT controller. **There are three sizes:**

| | AltMill 2×4 | AltMill 4×4 | AltMill 4×8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Work area (X × Y) | ~25 × 49 in | ~49 × 49 in (1265 × 1251 mm) | ~49.8 × 104 in (1265 × 2640 mm) |
| Z travel | ~5.5 in | ~5.5 in (one page: 174 mm) | ~210 mm |
| Max cutting speed | ~590-600 IPM | ~590-600 IPM | ~1,000 IPM Y, ~590 IPM X |
| Spindle | none included: 80 mm mount; optional 2.2 kW ER20 spindle, or the 2.2 kW ATC spindle | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |
| Rotary (optional) | Vortex rotary axis on the SLB-EXT's A output | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |
| Motion | NEMA 23 closed-loop steppers | as 2×4 | as 2×4 |

The figures come from Sienci's product and resources pages, which disagree with each other in places (the 4×4's Z: 5.5 in vs 174 mm; X and Y speeds). Confirm each figure against Sienci's current spec page or manual before committing a `.mch` (see Done means).

**Controller:** the SLB-EXT is a 32-bit board running **grblHAL**, usually driven by Sienci's gSender. That makes this post a grblHAL dialect, built on the grblHAL post in #710 (PR #715) rather than written from scratch.

**No new post file.** The AltMill machine files use `grblhal.cps` from #710, the way all the Tormach mills share `tormach.cps`. A separate `altmill.cps` is added only if something below cannot be a machine-file setting or a grblHAL post option. As of PR #715, the grblHAL post already does what an ATC needs: a plain `T<n> M6` on a line of its own, no G49 (the controller's measured tool length is kept), a `G53 G0 Z` lift when the machine file states `safe_retract` (the AltMill homes), and the first move after a change goes to XY before Z.

**Requirements** (on the machine files, or as small additions to the grblHAL post):
- **Tool change:** the most AltMill-specific part. The post must not depend on the sender: AltMill owners use gSender, and also alternatives such as ncSender. Two modes:
  - *Manual*: the sender intercepts `M6` and runs its own tool-change routine (pause, probe, and so on).
  - *ATC (firmware-handled)*: a `TC.macro` on the SLB-EXT runs `M6 Tn` inside grblHAL, which is transparent to the sender. This covers Sienci's ATC spindle and the **RapidChange ATC** ([rcatc-scripts-grblhal](https://github.com/greilick-industries/rcatc-scripts-grblhal): `TC.macro` runs on every `M6` with a valid tool, settings in `P200.macro`, grblHAL core 20240506 or newer).
  - In both modes the post emits a plain `M6 Tn` on a line of its own, as #710 already plans, with the length offset on the next line. It adds no sender-specific comments or macros, because some gSender versions reportedly rewrite `M6T1` even in passthrough.
  - A post option picks manual or ATC. With ATC, the machine file states the rack's pocket count and which tool numbers it holds, and any other tool is a manual change or a refusal by name. The tool length comes from the ATC's own measurement, so the post does not ask for a manual touch-off after an ATC change.
- **Units:** most AltMill users work in inches. The post honours G20/G21 from the setup and never mixes them.
- **Spindle:** the spindle is bought separately, so the machine file carries a default spindle (the 2.2 kW ER20, 24,000 rpm max, to be checked against Sienci's kit page) that the user can change. `S` words are clamped to the stated range, or refused by name if out of range.
- **Rotary (Vortex):** an A-axis rotary along X on the SLB-EXT's dedicated A output (closed-loop Vortex, gSender's "4th Axis Mode"). The older "Rotary Mode", which drives the rotary through the Y output, is not supported and is refused by name. Indexing and wrapping follow #714 and wait on it.
- **Out of scope:** laser (LaserBeam) and plasma add-ons.

**Done means:**
- `assets/machines/sienci-altmill-2x4.mch`, `sienci-altmill-4x4.mch` and `sienci-altmill-4x8.mch` exist, with travels, axis speeds, the default spindle and the rotary option. Every figure is sourced from Sienci's spec page or manual and cited in the decision file.
- All three are registered in `posting::MACHINES`, with tests in the style of the Tormach machine tests.
- The AltMill machines post through `grblhal.cps`, with goldens under `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/grblhal/` for a small pocket with a tool change on an AltMill machine, in both inch and mm. With an ATC rack stated, a tool outside the rack is handled as above. Any change needed in `grblhal.cps` keeps its existing goldens byte-exact.
- Without #714, any A word is refused by name. Once #714 lands, the Vortex is covered by its indexing goldens.
- The post passes a sender run and a real-machine dry run before it is trusted. I have an AltMill with an SLB-EXT, a RapidChange ATC and ncSender, and can run the goldens on that setup (ATC mode, ncSender).

body:
With several setups on screen, every origin triad looks alike - nothing in the viewport says whose zero is whose. Hover answers "what is this" only one gizmo at a time; the ask is to read it at a glance, and in a screenshot that goes onto a setup sheet.

**Shape wanted:** every origin gizmo labels itself at its origin. Each work-offset triad draws the entity name the Setup pane already uses (`G54` for the first setup, `Setup2/WCS` for the second) just below its projected origin, in a bright label color at the ordinary overlay-label size; the dimmed neutral world axes draw `World` in the same dim gray as their lines. Names ride `gizmos()`: always visible, and an offset hidden by the Models-pane eye - or the world-axes toggle - loses its name with its lines, so no label clutter survives a hidden gizmo. Only the axis-tip `X`/`Y`/`Z` letters keep the big font.

**Considered and dropped:** hover-only labels (not readable at a glance or screenshottable); per-tip offset glyphs (`G54 triad X` - six-plus glyphs per gizmo, clutter that buries the axes); coloring each offset's whole triad by setup (the axes' RGB channels already carry axis meaning).

**Already built:** PR #645 implements exactly this, pinned by `gizmo_tests` (world axes labeled `World`, each triad labeled with its own offset name, name stands at the origin not the tips, hidden offsets drop their names). This issue exists so that PR has the right number to close: the review on #645 caught that it cited #641 - the unrelated lathe grooving bug - by mistake.
